narration: We start at the input. A camera looks into the indoor scene, and a ray is cast through a pixel. Along that ray we take a 3D sample point p, shown as the yellow dot.
The point p is looked up in a multi-resolution feature grid. Coarse voxels at the top and fine voxels at the bottom each give a trilinearly interpolated feature vector for p.
The concatenated multi-resolution features, together with the raw coordinate of p, are fed into a small multi-layer perceptron.
The network outputs one signed distance value per object: an SDF for the floor, an SDF for the lamp, an SDF for the bed, and so on for every instance in the scene.
Taking the minimum across all those per-object distances gives the scene SDF, d-omega: the distance from p to the nearest surface of any object.
Each per-object SDF is converted into an object density profile, sigma. Along the ray, every object contributes its own density peak where its surface lies.
From the scene SDF we also accumulate the scene transmittance, T-omega, which falls off as the ray is blocked by whichever surface it meets first.
Multiplying each object density by that shared scene transmittance yields the occlusion-aware object opacity, O-hat. Peaks that sit behind another surface are suppressed.
The object opacities are supervised against the 2D instance masks with the loss L-O, so each object is only held responsible for the pixels where it is actually visible.
Transmittance multiplied by the scene density gives the volume rendering weight function, which says how much each sample along the ray contributes to the pixel.
Integrating with those weights renders a depth map, compared against the prior depth with the loss L-depth.
The same weights render a normal map, supervised by the loss L-normal.
The depth and normal targets come from a pretrained monocular prediction model, which supplies geometric cues the posed images alone cannot give.
The weights also render colour, and the reconstruction loss L-rec compares it with the captured RGB image.
Back on the field itself, the Eikonal loss L-SDF pushes the gradient norm of every per-object signed distance towards one, keeping each field a valid SDF.
Finally the regularisation loss L-reg penalises any object whose signed distance dips below the scene SDF, stopping objects from growing into the space occupied by their neighbours.
